این سرمایه‌گذاریِ انرژی بر فلان یا بهمان اندیشهٔ ناخودآگاه است که به آن امکان می‌دهد تا سطحِ خودآگاه سربرآورد یا برعکس به سوی ناخودآگاه واپس‌رانده شود. «چنین جریانی در دستگاه را که از نالذت آغاز می‌شود و لذت را نشانه می‌گیرد، آرزو می‌نامیم؛ گفته‌ایم که هیچ چیز جز یک آرزو توانِ به حرکت درآوردنِ دستگاه را ندارد و سیرِ برانگیختگی در آن به‌طورِ خودکار از طریقِ ادراک‌های لذت و نالذت تنظیم می‌شود.»
آن‌چه از این میان به خودآگاه می‌رسد «عواطف» است، یعنی کیفیتِ لذت یا نالذت (برآمده از واپس‌رانیِ یک آرزو، که بیشترِ اوقات جنسی است) که در موادِ اندیشه‌ایِ پرداخته‌شده توسطِ پیش‌آگاه نهفته است؛ پیش‌آگاهی که نشانه‌های زبان را از نظامِ یادمانی برمی‌گیرد.
خودآگاه در واقع همچون گیرنده‌ای برای ادراک‌های درونی رفتار می‌کند.
بدین اعتبار، می‌توان گفت که ناخودآگاه، از جمله با بُعدِ پیش‌آگاهِ خویش، نظامِ خودآگاه (Cs) را در بر می‌گیرد، زیرا هر آن‌چه خودآگاه است مرحلهٔ مقدماتیِ ناخودآگاه و مرحلهٔ میانیِ پیش‌آگاه دارد.
«ناخودآگاه دایرهٔ بزرگ‌تری است که دایرهٔ کوچک‌ترِ خودآگاه را در بر می‌گیرد؛ هر آن‌چه خودآگاه است، مرحلهٔ مقدماتیِ ناخودآگاه دارد، حال آن‌که ناخودآگاه می‌تواند در همین مرحله متوقف بماند… ناخودآگاه همان ساحتِ روانیِ به‌راستی واقعی است، که در سرشتِ درونی‌اش برای ما به همان اندازه ناشناخته است که ساحتِ واقعیِ جهانِ بیرونی، و از رهگذرِ داده‌های خودآگاه درست به همان اندازه ناقص به ما عرضه می‌شود که جهانِ بیرونی از طریقِ نشانه‌های اندام‌های حسیِ ما.»

*

اثر مُهرِ آفرینندهٔ خود را بر خود دارد.

تقلیل‌ناپذیریِ روحِ عقلانیِ او همچون امری ثابت پدیدار می‌شود؛ فرآوردهٔ رؤیاییِ خودِ او در آن موضوعِ پژوهش است و گوشه‌های برگزیده‌ای از روانش را بر ما آشکار می‌سازد. فروید برهنه و بی‌پرده است؛ کتاب از آستانهٔ آن‌چه به یک اثرِ علمی کیفیتِ اثری سترگ، اگر نگوییم کالت، برای علاقه‌مندانش می‌بخشد، فراتر رفته است. «تفسیر رؤیاها» کتابی است که فروید به واسطهٔ آن کردارِ تحلیلی را بنیان می‌نهد. چه بسیار عناصری که این‌جا بسط یافته‌اند، خود به کلیدهای همان سازوکارِ پیشِ رو بدل خواهند شد که هنوز در مکاتبِ تحلیل‌گرانِ امروزین محلِ بحث‌اند؟ گویی همه چیز از پیش نوشته شده بوده است؛ مطالعهٔ رؤیا نه‌تنها شاهراهی است که به مطالعهٔ پدیده‌های ناخودآگاه می‌انجامد، بلکه به پی‌ریزیِ شالودهٔ نظری‌ای نیز راه می‌برد که استواری‌اش هنوز چشمانِ ما را از شگفتی گشاد می‌کند. همین نقاطی را که در آن‌ها کشف و شدنِ کارِ او به هم مفصل‌بندی می‌شوند، می‌کوشیم در این گزارش نشانه بگیریم. البته، برای بیشترِ ما این خوانش نخستین خوانش نیز هست و به زیباترین شیوه ورودِ ما را به پهنهٔ نظریِ روان‌کاوی آغاز می‌کند. آیا روان‌کاوی بدونِ این دستاورد آینده‌ای می‌داشت؟ هیچ چیز از این نامطمئن‌تر نیست…

در پیِ این کارِ نخست، گروهِ ما کشفِ خود از امرِ ناخودآگاه را با تداوم‌بخشیدن به تأملاتش از طریقِ مطالعهٔ «توتم و تابو»، کتابی نوشتهٔ زیگموند فروید و منتشرشده در سال ۱۹۲۳، دنبال می‌کند. در این ماجراجوییِ تازه، آرزو داریم به سنجشِ درستی و اعتبارِ مفاهیمِ نیرومندِ روان‌کاوی ادامه دهیم. بدین منظور، خواهیم کوشید «روزآمدیِ» انگاره‌های فرویدی را در رویکردی انسان‌شناختی بسنجیم که در آن دیالکتیکِ میانِ کارکردِ فرد و شکل‌گیریِ جوامعِ ما همچون نیروی محرکه عمل خواهد کرد. زیرا چنان‌که ژان-ژاک روسو می‌گفت: «انسان با جامعه سرِ ناسازگاری ندارد؛ اما بدان مایل نیز نیست. او در درونِ خویش جوانه‌هایی دارد که چون پرورش یابند، به فضیلت‌های اجتماعی و گرایش‌های اجتماعی بدل می‌شوند؛ اما آن‌ها تنها قوه‌هایی بیش نیستند. کمال‌پذیری، فضیلت‌های اجتماعی و دیگر قوایی که انسانِ طبیعی به‌صورتِ بالقوه دریافت کرده بود، هرگز نمی‌توانستند به‌خودیِ خود رشد و گسترش یابند» (گفتارِ دوم، بخشِ نخست).

۳ نوامبر ۲۰۰۹

en.title: Nature / Counter-Nature: Does Wisdom Have a Role to Play?
en.executive_summary: Is it collective wisdom or individual wisdom that enables the definition of a nature / counter-nature perimeter? Between 30 June 2012 and 30 June 2013, a working group composed of Anne-Gaëlle Burban, Hassan Makaremi, Emmanuelle Bour-Poitrinal,…
en.body_markdown:
Is it collective wisdom or individual wisdom that enables the definition of a nature / counter-nature perimeter?

Between 30 June 2012 and 30 June 2013, a working group composed of Anne-Gaëlle Burban, Hassan Makaremi, Emmanuelle Bour-Poitrinal, Isabelle Prudhomme, Yoann Murguet, and Esfandiar Attaran set itself the objective of entering into the nature / counter-nature problematic through the production of several texts.

Thus, without any apparent logical sequence, and flirting instead with the spontaneity of free association, there emerges from this corpus an aleatory yet no less profound study.

This anthology, akin to a logbook, is a collective essay that seeks to delineate the issues underlying the nature / counter-nature dialectic—one likely to interest psychoanalysts, anthropologists, visual artists, poets, psychologists, architects, engineers, and other curious enquirers into human history alike.

Something of Death Belongs Only to Man

Yoann MURGUET

Approaching the problematic of nature / counter-nature from a psychoanalytic standpoint requires a few useful detours towards universal notions. Known for their apparent simplicity, the notions of the living, nature, the natural, life, and the soul… will lay the foundations of our reflection. We shall see that the problematic of nature / counter-nature concerns Man alone, encompassing the notions of humanity and the Subject. We shall also see, once we have isolated it, the role of human language in relation to our questioning.

Is the living in motion? Can it be said to be immutable, transgressive, governed by laws? Is the living world one or multiple? What purpose does Life have? Present knowledge, under the aegis of biology and genetics, teaches us that an invisible world governs us. From the definition of the living examined under the lens of scholars, it emerges that it is sustained by organised, programmed, unicellular or multicellular organisms endowed with a capacity for reproduction, whose purpose appears to be essentially the continuity of the life of the cell or of the organism in which it participates. Is the reproduction of life identical to its parent? It would seem not. This continuity of life occurs through the modification of genetic expression. The cell owes much to its formidable adaptability to the environment. Programmatic encoding may well be immutable, yet its still little-known variations in expression seem infinite. For the moment, we remain without any genuine understanding of this phenomenon, though observation has shown us the existence of a dialectic between genetics and the space-time proper to the organism. One then speaks of a capacity for self-modification.

We say of the natural that it goes without saying; by this we mean that it is the mark of a scrupulous adherence to the ordering of a system. From this natural state proper to a system, one can predict what is and what will be. The faculty to deviate from the natural is nil if the system is by nature incapable of extracting itself in any manner whatsoever from the thrust that governs it, if it is not endowed with a power of mastery, of conscientisation, of shared conceptual elaborations (knowledge), or with a tendency towards self-modification. Without any of these attributes, the living organism is doomed to disappearance. Whatever its nature, it is often unintelligible: the mark of the Real. Often, knowledge of the nature of a thing is reduced to the act of predicting an event. Let us simply bear in mind that prediction is not equivalent to knowledge as a whole; it is merely a particular case of it. This abusive restriction of predictive knowledge holds sway in the contemporary scientific world: logical positivism. This will undoubtedly have to evolve somewhat. The natural is merely a qualitative state of perfection in the intrinsic functioning of the Nature of an object.

Yet the living has several scales of study; it is impossible for us to reduce it, and each scale allows us to apprehend one facet of it. That current studies accord primacy to the infinitely small or the infinitely large in addressing questions at the contours of the Real does not constitute proof that the positivist paradigm is the right one. The study of superficial layers does not have the same impact, and surpassing classical epistemology is necessary to advance further into our problematic. This question of the living has long been approached by Man from less restrictive and more reflective perspectives. For example, in Aristotle, life is prior and in becoming by nature. This return to such a mode of reflection seems here to surpass in complexity the conclusions drawn from the biological sciences. The living is distinguished from the non-living by its quality of being animate: what is animate is living, and consequently what is not animate is non-living. This definition in Aristotle is closely bound up with that of the soul: the soul is the first actuality of an organised body. In Aristotle, the notion of the soul belongs solely to the living; it is breath and structuring force, found across the vegetal, animal, and human kingdoms, and may be vegetative and/or sensitive and/or locomotive and/or intellective.

The vegetative soul aims solely at its own production and its reproduction, understood as the perpetuation of the species. The sensitive soul allows for a sensing of external stimuli. The locomotive soul enables certain bodies to move. The intellective soul concerns humankind and, through its complexity, surpasses the other typologies.

One may conclude from Aristotle that all souls, whatever they may be, are animated by a thrust towards realisation of unequal value, optimised according to the genus of the body they possess.

In animals and plants, the faculty to pierce the structural shell that animates them is impossible unless subjected to external constraints. What is meant here are modifications resulting from major changes in the environment. These may be physical or chemical, the consequences of an environmental mutation. In its general acceptation, it is appropriate to regard these souls as wholly natural.

The case of Man is altogether different according to Aristotle. His soul belongs to all four types, the last being proper to him alone. The first three place him on the same footing as the others, whereas the fourth singularises him to the utmost degree. It is this singularity that interests our reflection. Man is endowed with intelligence, a complex language, an imaginary, and a capacity for belief, to which one may add a psychic structuring of his own. Therein lies his potential to deviate from the natural order—a possible threat to his survival.

Man thus possesses a language, a tangible symbolic medium capable of accounting for the other characteristics proper to his species. We know of this language that it is a sum of signs carried by several media (written, verbal, gestural, olfactory, artistic, etc.); it serves for the expression and communication of thoughts with other members of his species. This language becomes shared through submission to common rules (syntax) and the will to transmit meaning (semantics). Man appears to borrow this language from the common pool, although individually he weaves privileged ties with certain words (master signifier) as so many anchors of the Subject defining him in the face of the world’s complexity.

Words are for him vectors of meaning; in this way he enters into a dialectic with his environment. His individual or collective productions impact and rival nature; he does not merely draw inspiration from it, he modifies it. We shall speak of an artefact to distinguish what is produced beyond his body through the channel of language—reflecting the activity of his intelligence and sensibility—and of psychosomatics as the effect upon the body of a language structure tied to his psychic life.

The articulation of this latter notion with language underscores the presence of another linguistic agency: the Other as the secret of signifiers in Lacan.

To study the human species in its relations to the nature / counter-nature problematic, we must consider what, from the vestiges of its past and the products issuing from its contemporary dynamics, enters into common share. If there is a tendency towards counter-nature, we ought to be able to bring to light, through the two phenomena of the artefact and psychosomatics, a tendency towards the annihilation of the group and of the Subject.

The aim here is not to argue the morality of this or that act, but simply to illuminate the elements of the human group or of the individual that lead it to its ruin, to its unravelling. Let us start from the following postulate: that which is against nature is that which harms the continuation of life.

The notion of the artefact will be addressed succinctly in order to introduce a forthcoming reflection. As for the notion of psychosomatics, it will be developed in another article.

Examples of artefacts:

- Positive scientific artefact:

Beyond symbolisation, the Real stands encamped. The irresistible need to understand would take birth at its borders. Does the human adventure not teach us to fill the void of knowledge and heal the wound of humanity’s wounded narcissism?

The time when genius emerges can only be the precursory and transformative moment turning an old worldview into a new, more fertile one that guarantees a civilisational surpassing. Is it not said of scientists that they discover only what “is”, that they do not invent? Yet if they do not invent, we can recognise in genius at the very least the faculty of laying the milestones of a new path on the basis of existing concepts. Thus, from time to time, we surpass civilisational acquisitions. The concept of emergence supports this idea; it postulates at the outset that the world is constituted by degrees of organisation/integration. Their number is not predefined; one therefore assumes N levels of organisation in the world. To understand emergence, it suffices to accept that level N+1 is constituted by the elements of level N when they organise together. It suffices that the wholes constituted by this higher-complexity organisation be stable and possess properties of their own (different from those of their type-N components).

Political artefact 1:

Unsavoury, simplistic, and radical, war participates—to a certain extent and without masking its morbid character—in a redistribution, “a new deal”. Recourse to war does not necessarily entail a paradigm shift.

War enables the resumption of the dominant paradigm, stripped of the questions surrounding its legitimacy.

Political artefact 2:

Conservatism, defined as an attachment to current values, cannot tolerate the emergence of the new. Yet societies claiming allegiance to or approximating this ideological model produce a form of evolution over time and lay claim to progressivism. Even so, this is not the progress that humanity so sorely needs, but rather a kind of complexification of ramifications operating on the basis of prevailing knowledge. Every value produces caricatures of itself, going so far as to border on fascism.

The death drive comes to our aid in defining the concept of nature / counter-nature. Here, it gives new meaning and illumination to the evolution of life and its perils (beyond the pleasure principle).

As long as signifiers exist, as long as they accumulate around the common bedrock of a civilisation, there is life. Any halt, or anything that may impede the emergence of new signifiers, constitutes so many signals of imminent danger, of a hypothetical death. The process of symbolisation cannot be considered finished. It is the imprint of life, the mark of the continuity of humankind, the narrative of its knowledge, its history, and its movements. How could we characterise its trajectory, its displacements in time and space? What future might we suppose for it? The question remains open.

A symbolic order devoted to a constant renewal of its terms through the principle of exploration and surpassing its acquisitions appears to be the principal movement that characterises it. Yet one can sometimes witness entire swathes of a new symbolic world emerge; they carry in germ the power of the living, the renewal of all terms, and participate henceforth in the architecture of the new common bedrock, becoming master signifiers for a time. At other times, the constant movement that animates it finds no outlet other than the degradation of these originary terms. One then sees emerging within already defined worlds a myriad of compositions, every bit as surprising as if they were novelties in their own right. The lure is effective: it readily substitutes itself for that need for renewal which life demands. At work in such a case is a contrary action, a morbid drive that substitutes itself, through the play of illusion, for the tendency towards perpetual and regenerative movement. By adding a new complexity to the old matrix, the death drive sustains the illusion of a progressive movement and brings about the annulment of vital energy. Movement is no longer fed by the new, owing its displacement solely to its momentum, until it comes to a complete halt. It is indeed this force of inertia that produces the illusion of perpetual motion and of the grand march of progress. Its halt, if one may speak of a halt, seems to occur at the expense of the sources of life.

The desire for evolution is not, however, a desire common to all human beings; one still finds in the most primitive tribes, remaining intact, a profound and acknowledged absence of this desire. Evolution brings about the death of this state of inertia.

It appears that progress tends to sideline and dissolve the other modes of life that Man has managed to develop throughout his existence. Progress tends to impose itself as the sole way of life on earth for our species; will Man be able to tame the dangers with which this thirst for change confronts him? What qualities must he develop in order to take charge of his destiny without suffering from it?

LINK:

WHAT DOES THE STUDY OF LIMITS TEACH US?

"Where Does the Limit Stop?"

Hassan MAKAREMI

The question of the limit, the border, the neighbourhood, the out-of-reach, the beyond... from the psychoanalytic point of view, can be explained through the five key elements: life, death, the Signifier, the signified, and the Phallus. Next, the limit of our experience—the Real—will summon us. “Indeed, we need not be surprised by this; the Real is at the limit of our experience,” says J. Lacan in Seminar IV, page 31. Let us set out in search of limits across different fields of our knowledge and learning to date, in quest of “limit” signifiers in the depths of time, space, the universe, life, Man, the speaking Subject, the body, the psyche, the possible…

To begin with the relations between the signifier, the signified, life, death, and the role of the phallus in order to understand the domains of each and their interferences. How, starting from this limit—“death”—can the support of the signifier exist? Ultimately, we cannot escape this question: “Outside the ‘limit of the signifier’, is the identification of another ‘limit’ possible?”

Jacques Lacan, speaking of S. Freud, specifies—I quote Seminar IV, page 48: “This is most certainly what Freud brought us under the term death instinct. It is a matter of this limit of the signified which is never attained by any living being, or even never attained at all, save in an exceptional, probably mythical case…”. Let us comment on this sentence, and first: what does the signifier mean? An acoustic image, the origin of language, that which makes primal repression possible.

J. Lacan, in Écrits, page 575: “The signifying chain was inaugurated by primordial symbolisation.”

S. Freud hopes to find what is psychically innate through the analytic procedure, through the emergence of signifiers; I quote Freud in The Interpretation of Dreams: “We may hope to succeed, through the analysis of dreams, in coming to know the archaic heritage of Man, in discovering what is psychically innate…”. The analysis of dreams by listening to the Subject’s discourse: such, according to Freud, is the tool of archaeological excavation for reaching into the deepest strata of humanity, going where no tool other than the Symbolic dimension exists: signifiers enable us to do so. Beyond signifiers, there are letters, numbers, and pure symbols that will be the subject of another investigation, such as the importance of letters in Freud’s dream of Irma or the use of symbolic letters or numbers in sacred texts.

The relation between the signified and the Signifier was presented by J. Lacan as S/s. It is said that for one signifier S, there are several signifieds across different subjects as well as for the same subject at different moments. Yet there is only one signifier that can have the same signified for everyone and at every moment: death as a point of no return, definitive death—no other interpretation is possible. J. Lacan, Seminar IV, page 48, specifies for us: “What lies at the foundation of the existence of the signifier, of its presence in the world, we shall place right there in our schema, as an effective surface of the signifier where it reflects, as it were, what one may call the last word of the signified—that is to say, of life, of lived experience, of the flow of emotions, of the libidinal flow. It is death, insofar as it is the support, the basis, the operation of the Holy Spirit by which the signifier exists.”

Where does the signified stop? As J. Lacan specifies: “this limit of the signified which is never attained by any living being, or even never attained at all, save in an exceptional, probably mythical case…”. Bearing in mind that for certain experiences in this world, words fail. “The sexual relationship is impossible”, or rather its rendering into a signifier is impossible, as is the jouissance of the other. I return to Lacan and the exceptional cases: “this limit of the signified which is never attained by any living being, or even never attained at all, save in an exceptional, probably mythical case”. We may already speak of the different categories of experience: mystics, subjects who have undergone near-death experiences (EMI / NDE), prophets, subjects experiencing hallucinations (illusion, hallucination, febrile state), drugged subjects, high-level athletes, those returning from a comatose state, and certain cases of hypnosis or altered states of consciousness. They all say that they are unable to explain their experience adequately in words, which makes receiving their speech—and, where applicable, interpreting it—very difficult.

What Prophets, mystics, and psychotics have in common is that the link between the signifier and the signified is severed. For the psychotic, the chain of speech presents itself without limit and without vectorisation. Psychosis causes the link between cause and effect to be lost; signifiers break away from reality. What is the boundary between delusion and non-delusion? On the one hand, the delusion of the neurotic, who knows that he is deluded because the signifier–signified division is still intact; on the other hand, the delusion of the psychotic and the discourses of mystics and prophets, who harbour no doubt because the Signifier has become real. Hence the two testimonies, in the Bible: “In the beginning was the Word”, and in the Qur'an: “Be, and it becomes”.

Metaphysics renders death floating, uncertain, pushes it back, and causes it to be invented. It gives rise to the invention of concepts such as life after death, the soul, the spirit, and reincarnation. During the period of adolescence, hesitation over fundamental questions—about life, about death, where do I come from, what is the point of it all…—and the effect of the quest for identity stem, on the one hand, from this relation of the link between signifieds and concepts, and, on the other hand, from identification, from the effect of the signifier or of the (?) Name-of-the-Father.

A few words on the formation of the unconscious and on the role of the Phallus.

Castration: Discovery of the limit

Frustration Privation

Privation: discovery of the fields of lack

Frustration: discovery of the fields of existence

J. Lacan specifies: “the phallus is the symbol of an imaginary object”.

Castration: symbolic lack of an imaginary object (e.g. symbolic lack of the phallus as an imaginary object); according to J. Lacan: “castration is the submission of the subject to the signifier”. To name it, to give a signifier, to bring life into view. (?)

Frustration: imaginary lack of a real object (e.g. I have the impression that I shall run out of oxygen…).

Privation: real lack of a symbolic object (e.g. being deprived of the fabric of the mother’s dress).

The phallus, that difference which makes the difference:

Phallus

Mother Child

The Phallus is therefore the signifier that has no signified.

Our experience and its limit: the Real, some examples.

1 - Despite the clear definition of structure—neurosis, perversion, and psychosis—we encounter the borderline state…: borderline situation, borderline patient, limit of the analysable, limit between structures, limit between pathology and non-pathology, to such an extent that in DSM-IV [SDM IV], the American Psychiatric Association does not assign a precise pathological name, but proposes (?) a link between treatments and symptoms.

2 - For Man, which of these signifiers is the most accurate? Individual, subject of desire, person, citizen, ego, first name + surname or family name, self-consciousness, social being, or, following S. Freud, frontier being. What limit can be given to him in order to designate him?

3 - Internal reality and external reality: boundary of the body.

Unconscious

Body

Conscious

Preconscious unconscious image of the body

J. Lacan: “The body makes the bed of the Other through the operation of the signifier”.

The Unconscious is structured like a language. This structure defines the typology of the fundamental organisation of signifiers. The formation of the unconscious during a subject’s life, as a system that operates with signifiers, binds the unconscious to two basic elements on the outside: the body and the conscious. The unconscious is structured like a language and “A” [the Other] is the treasury of signifiers, for if it were structured upon signifieds, it would vary over the course of a subject’s life; the most solid foundation is the Name-of-the-Father, an unchanging signifier which founds the subject’s identity.

4 - The speed of light: the accepted limit of the (physical) sciences is the speed of light, provisionally accepted as the basis of calculations, theories, hypotheses, as well as of our imaginings. To my knowledge, there is no screenplay, film, or artistic production that develops the moment of crossing this limit of light, though there are examples illustrating the moment of arrival in that beyond of the speed of light. One imagines the before and the after, but not the during.

5 - Some examples of the frontier effect and the limit in the social field:

5.1 - Cloning as the limit of the individual. This is the first time that this

two physical persons are the same individual with the same definition of the bond between generations. In other words, cloning breaks the limit of the other, the chain of generations—father and child, brother and sister—the question of the living and of death, the Name-of-the-Father, and one’s place in space-time.

Cloning stands at the end of a chain of taboos in our history: the touching of another’s body by someone other than a family member, seeing it naked, performing an autopsy upon it, transplanting organs, listening to intimacy, to others, and to their dreams, transplanting an organ derived from a clone, and finally cloning the human being. The fundamental problem is not each new stage, but knowing for what reason, to what utility, and to what objective. The fundamental question is: how do we halt the procedure? How do we alter course? Until now, our individual attempts to go to the threshold of our limits were individual thresholds, limits of the human being: examples in the circus, the limit-experience of solitude, the Olympic Games, space travel. These experiences were viewed favourably by us, whereas cloning is a collective affair.

5.2 - Reification of death: without going into detail, I would point out to you that, upon returning from the experience of the concentration camps, discourse—putting things into words—becomes impossible for subjects.

5.3 - Legal experts, in their reports, use fewer than a hundred clearly identified signifiers, bordering on mathematics; the closer the judgement approaches serious cases, the more precise the signifiers become.

5.4 - Phenomenon of the struggle against borders: Médecins du Monde, Médecins Sans Frontières. On the one hand, globalisation; on the other hand, the absence of borders—two camps fighting each other. Yet both speak of abolishing borders.

5.5 Borders of Europe: I quote Le Monde of 5 January (YEAR), Casanova, concerning Europe and Turkey: “…one sees clearly here why the question of borders leads to that of the nature of Europe…”.

5.6 Money: a well-quantified signifier, which always says the same thing, can become the God of globalisation on the one hand and life without borders on the other. Alas, choosing money is simpler. Example: the Dollar and the Euro in place of a common social project. For as Tolstoy tells us in the preface to his book War and Peace—I quote from memory: “I wonder why the wicked unite more easily than the good”. Money is more palpable, more concrete than life: the opposite of death.

6 - Limit and mathematics:

A I I I I B

1/2+1/4+1/8+1/16….= a

1/2+1/2*(1/2+1/4+1/8+1/16….)=a

1/2+1/2*a=a a =1

To define the limit, mathematical theory uses infinity—a symbol, a signifier with as many signifieds as there are human beings.

III - The limit is ultimately the limit of the signifier. Let us take an example: two subjects are speaking to one another; the discussion bears on the topic “What is the universe?”. They share a hundred signifiers in common. Their capacity to understand each other and convey the message is very limited. The same case with 10,000 shared signifiers yields a different field of vision and comprehension. The quantity of shared signifiers is the sole measurable element of limits. If we broaden this reasoning, extending it to multiple speaking beings and even to 6 billion, and add the concept of time—the totality of signifiers produced, disseminated, and understood—then we can imagine the volume of the vast field of the limit in the future. On the one hand, the number of living speaking beings is increasing, and their communications likewise; they learn to speak different languages and share more and more signifiers; on the other hand, ancient signifiers are rediscovered through research. Fields of research exchange ever more signifiers with one another, and the volume of signifiers in circulation via modern technology (the internet) is rising. This is the definable meaning of progress, of evolution, of advancement: to widen the frontier of signifiers, to push back death. A war between death and life—life, the quantity of signifiers.

Total of signifiers

1 - Discovery of lost signifiers

2 - 7 billion human beings alive today, 13 billion in total

3 - Increase in exchanges between languages

4 - Increase in the speed of transmission

5 - Written memory enables more signifiers to be preserved

6 - Invented signifiers: SNCF, RATP, NATO

7 - Scientific and technical fields… 4 words for the name of an insect, for example…

Time

Sublime Wisdom.

Anne-Gaëlle Burban, November 2012

Let us start from the idea that individual wisdom is constructed both with and against the collective wisdom transmitted ever since the human being became capable of emitting and receiving symbolisations. In a certain way, language is then perceived as the vector of this ancestral wisdom and serves to curb certain passages à l’acte, which will instead be sublimated through symbolisation. This symbolisation has the function of making intimate emotional perceptions present to the widest possible number. The perimeter—or rather the edge—between nature and counter-nature would thus be traced by words, music, art, poetry, dance, mathematics, and the more personal production of symptoms, fantasies…

Before going any further, it seems important to me to attempt to define certain key terms of this problematic. First, we shall ask: what is wisdom? Is it sublimated Man? How does he dialogue with the ideal agencies (ego-ideal and ideal ego)? What are the interactions between the intimate and the public, the individual and the collective?

We shall also see how language and the unconscious play a primordial role in the individuation of the subject within a given society.

Finally, we shall be able to establish and analyse the impacts of what, from the standpoint of psychoanalysis, belongs to the order of nature and what pertains to counter-nature in Man.

The concept of sublimation actually originates in sexuality: it answers the necessity of explaining how non-sexual manifest contents (for instance, scientific or artistic works) nonetheless have their source in unconscious sexuality and draw their expressive force from the libido.

What is sublimated? Aggressiveness, primitive sexuality, repressed desires—that is to say, everything that composes the unconscious and nourishes its manifestations.

Here is the definition of sublimation given by the Dictionnaire de la psychanalyse et de la micropsychanalyse: “a sexual or aggressive drive, inhibited as to its aim, sees its object-aim desexualised or de-aggressivised and socially, particularly culturally, valued.” (Fanti, 1983, p. 107). One thus understands that sublimation is grounded in a complex secondary elaboration. It results from work that takes place essentially at the preconscious level. The necessary transformations undergone by unconscious aggressive potential in order to enable the individual’s social dimension highlight the regulatory role of the preconscious. Concretely, sublimation is a process transforming something that is clearly characterised at the unconscious level—something typical of aggressiveness or sexuality—into something that is no longer so at the manifest level.

This localisation of the dynamics of sublimation at the preconscious level already allows us to put forward the hypothesis that each subject carries within himself a fragment of collective wisdom enabling him to transform his unconscious aggressive drives into social symbolic productions.

Yet how is this preconscious barrier formed? Does the individual, in the history of his psychic structuring, have a responsibility, a power, or simply the ability to play an active role? Or, on the contrary, is everything inherited from hereditary culture through language? What is each person’s room for manoeuvre in playing with his social determinisms? In other words, is everything decided before the age of 5, or may one hope to continue evolving afterwards? What of major, moderate, and minor delinquents, murderers, and other actors of the passage à l’acte? Moreover, are we not all petty delinquents when, more or less consciously, we continue to consume without recycling, when we drive without concerning ourselves with our ecological footprint…? Is their fate—our fate—knotted forever?

What can culture, common wisdom, citizenship, or psychoanalysis do to help us develop our capacity for sublimation?

Freud, in his work Civilisation and Its Discontents [Malaise dans la culture], published in 1930, asserts in particular that in his view:

culture is built upon drive renunciation, for living together presupposes a restriction of individual freedom or conformism;

respect for social demands is ensured first by the father and then by the “superego” (the internalised father, the faculty of self-constraint, moral conscience); the tension between the “id” (pleasure principle) and the “ego” (reality principle), between egoism (self-love) and altruism (love of others), is the source of the sense of guilt and of moral conscience; these social demands manifest themselves in morality and in religion, including in beauty, cleanliness, and order: these discourses attempt to legitimise and ensure the renunciation of egoistic pleasure.

As partisans of creative intelligence, let us wager that sublimation can be learned, sculpted, and even at times heal us by freeing us from repetitive (creaticidal) patterns, through unveiling the unconscious causes of human aggressiveness. Comparable to a negative and destructive excitation, this Thanatos drive is common to all and is built for each individual upon lived experiences memorised and internalised since earliest childhood, which must be expressed in order to free oneself from them (or at least neutralise their destructive power). Obviously, not all lived experiences are memorised. In order to be repressed and internalised, an experience must be particularly intense, repetitive, or conflictual; for example, a given experience of oral satisfaction is memorised because it interacts with narcissistic fantasies and provokes a vivid sensation of plenitude, while a given experience of castration is memorised because it is conflictual to the point of engendering representations of annihilation.

Let us return for a moment to the history of this notion of sublimation. In Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Freud considers sublimation to be one of the three paths of elaboration and discharge of repressed infantile sexuality, taking its place (in the adult) alongside the neurotic and perverse paths. In Instincts and Their Vicissitudes [Pulsions et destin des pulsions] (1915), he makes it a vicissitude of the drive, on the same footing as reversal into its opposite, turning round upon the subject’s own self, and repression.

In The Ego and the Id (1923), one finds a model of the sublimation of the libido. It is founded on identification and has narcissism as its pivot. The objects of the sexual drives are internalised (= identification); they thus become desexualised components of the ego and are cathected as such (= narcissistic cathexis). Consequently, the id henceforth loves the ego just as it sexually desired external objects. Narcissistic libido can then shift and cathect non-sexual and culturally valued objects. The energy of the ego is “a desexualised libido [of which] one may also say that it is sublimated energy, in the sense that it makes its own the principal intention of Eros, which consists in uniting and binding…” (p. 217).

Later, for Melanie Klein, the sublimation of aggressiveness is anchored in the depressive position and makes it possible, through symbolisations and the staging of fantasies, to repair the object destroyed by sadistic drives. Let us note in passing an aspect of Kleinian thought that is particularly interesting for anyone who is also interested in Lacan (in his Seminar on Anxiety in particular) and in the sublimation of the void (more precisely, of a lack created by the signifier). It is the void created by the destruction of the object that arouses the anxiety impelling restorative sublimation—namely the equation:

lack or destruction of a - feeling of Void - anxiety - restorative sublimation

Winnicott extends Kleinian views by taking broad account of the environment: according to him, sublimation is rooted in transitional phenomena which, when the mother is good enough, allow the child’s creativity to repair what his aggressive drives have damaged or destroyed.

This is also what Sabina Spielrein raised as early as 1913 in her article entitled “Destruction as the Cause of Coming into Being”, published in Internationale Zeitschrift für ärztliche Psychoanalyse, I.

Today, as Daniel Lysek emphasises (Bollettino dell'Istituto Italiano di Micropsicoanalisi, no. 22, Turin, Tirrenia Stampatori, 1997), genuine sublimation, as psychoanalysts understand it, always retains a link with the drive dynamism that lies at its origin; even when it appears far removed from it, a sublimated manifestation remains permanently fed by the originary drive thrust.

At this stage, one might then put forward that collective wisdom encourages lack and anxiety as a natural and necessary condition for the survival of the Human species. On the contrary, at the level of a subject, the lack of lack would be the counter-natural thing par excellence.

That said, renunciation cannot occur too early; it must be the fruit of a profound knowledge of the cause and give way to a reasoned liquidation through close encounter with limits. It is limits that teach us life. This holds only for the subject. The group has its prophets and other explorers to instruct it. Can the group, moreover, take the risks run by a lone individual?

Bridling, seducing Thanatos (in the etymological sense se-ducere: to lead to oneself, to divert from its primary aim) without seeking to kill it. By what alchemy can one succeed in profoundly sublimating Thanatos into Eros without engendering unconscious conflicts? Where must this take place, in which topography: conscious? Preconscious? Unconscious? How can we act? How has nature managed, for better or worse, to combine this sexual dialectic between Eros and Thanatos while preserving the species and enabling humanity to continue evolving?

To go further, allow me then this syllogism worthy of a La Palice truism:

All Men are aggressive, lacking, and desiring,

now all wise men are Men,

therefore all wise men are aggressive, lacking, and desiring!

In other words, what counts above all is what one is going to do with this primary aggressiveness, this death drive, or this anxiety. How can we succeed in managing it so that something else blossoms—something that carries within itself the same power, yet whose object-aim has changed and converted positively without collateral damage? And how can we be certain not to cause (oneself) neurotic malaise? For when sublimation fails, drive potential transmutes and fixes itself into a psychic or psychosomatic symptom.

Does the answer lie in individual neurosis acting as a veritable universal cap [calotte] before the great prohibitions (death, incest) and the social anxiety of the withdrawal of love?

It is in any case towards this answer that S. Freud makes his way in his work Totem and Taboo.

Are we condemned to live with our neurosis in order to survive socially? If so, how can we succeed in transmuting our unconscious drives into creative productions, thus avoiding defensive neurotic elaboration or perverse discharge?

As Michel de Montaigne said in his Essays, how to live aptly [à propos]?

Incidentally, among the effects of an analysis, the opening towards sublimation occupies a by no means negligible place. Indeed, the talking cure, as Anna O. liked to call it, enables this in-out, this back-and-forth movement, and this displacement from one stratum to another.

Indeed, language is one of the keys, and symbolisation another pivot, in embodying an artificial, cathartic, and salvific path of decongestion enabling us to draw closer to our desire and its cause, in objet a.

In the chapter on the causes of desire, in his Seminar on Anxiety, Jacques Lacan tells us on p. 121: “it is the notion of an outside prior to a certain internalisation, which is situated at a, before the subject, at the locus of the Other, grasps himself in the specular form, at x, which introduces for him the distinction between the ego and the non-ego.”

Is psychoanalysis then against nature [contre nature], in the sense in which Sacha Guitry said he was against women—right up against them [tout contre]?

TITLE + IP

: OCTOBER AND DECEMBER 2012

Starting point:

The question, “is it collective wisdom or individual wisdom that can enable the definition of the nature / counter-nature perimeter?” leads me to several reflections on the subject of individual wisdom.

My hypothesis: individual wisdom would pass through assuming one’s desire for power (or will to power?) and assuming the correlative castrations and limitations. As if one’s own symbolic castration could stand as the reference of references, or the value of values, notably when it is “crossed” with the symbolic castrations of others…

This notion of symbolic castration will therefore remain to be defined, as well as that of the desire for power / will to power.

The notion of castration:

For Lacan, the notion of castration is more readily used than that of the castration complex. Defined “as a symbolic operation that determines a subjective structure”[1].

The singular subjective structure would be the result of the symbolic operation, which bears upon the phallus, not as a real object, but as an imaginary one.

“The child, girl or boy, wants to be the phallus in order to capture his mother’s desire (this is the first moment of the Oedipus complex). The prohibition of incest (second moment) must dislodge the child from this ideal position of the maternal phallus. This prohibition is the act of the symbolic father—that is to say, of a law whose mediation must be ensured by the mother’s discourse. Yet it does not target the child alone; it also targets the mother and, for that reason, is understood by the child as castrating her.”[2] We may understand that one castration is structurally correlative to another, in the primary relation to the love-object.

In the third moment, “the real father intervenes—the one who has the phallus (more precisely, the one who, for the child, is supposed to have it), the one who, in any case, makes use of it and makes himself preferred by the mother.”[3] The child, who has renounced being the phallus, will identify with the father: perhaps it is here that sexual difference and the correlative sexed identifications intervene.

The boy renounces being the phallus, and also renounces making use of the one he has, which does not “measure up”, deferring this use in time. The displacement in relation to the primary object will still remain to be carried out later, the temptation to return or regress towards the mother being unconsciously renegotiated in adolescence, as the subject grapples notably with identification with the father.

The girl likewise renounces being the mother’s phallus, and then renounces having the father’s phallus; there remains the third operation, which would be the renunciation of the temptation to be the father’s phallus.

At this price, the sexual act with another subject would then become possible.

Could these stages not be summed up in a relation to being and having (the phallus), endlessly transitory and renegotiated in the relation to the other—whether the father, the mother, or their substitutes subsequently?

Let us understand substitutes in the sense that they take up imaginary, symbolic, and/or real traits from our primary identifications.

Not to be the phallus, or not to be the object of the other’s desire, not to be the object that the other lacks.

Not to have the phallus, or not to “claim to be its master”[4].

Would this “not” refer back to an act of conscientisation, of active and symbolic renunciation, always to be re-enacted within this structural dynamic (unconscious, at least in part) that would map itself onto every invested human relationship? And perhaps even simply in the relation of oneself to oneself? Which would therefore pass through a separation, a division.

We encounter this notion of separation repeatedly in a work by Denise Morel entitled “Psychoanalysis and Cancer”.

One of her major hypotheses is stated thus: the subject suffering from cancer “offers us an open testimony of his non-access to symbolic castration”[5].

The notion of transitivism illustrates well this non-operative symbolic castration: when the other is afflicted in his body, in the imaginary I am afflicted through the play of the mirror. “I am so close to my child that what touches him touches me—and, as D. Morel recalls, we are all someone’s children, (…) we regard as our children so many beings who are not, that this sentence applies to a great many relationships”[6]. The suffering image of the other would come to enact both a differentiation and a separation, sometimes difficult to symbolise, passing through anxiety—castration anxiety (or anxiety of fragmentation?).

The person who resorts to somatisation would displace this stake of separation: rather than accomplishing it with the other, it would be enacted with oneself and one’s own body, or at least a part of it. As if sacrificing oneself to an affliction upon one’s body would help spare the other or the relationship with him.

Another hypothesis might consist in associating the idea of nature with that of the body, and counter-nature with what the body “undergoes” (illness, shock, accident, trauma, symptom, means of defence against whatever does violence to it or assaults it, whether in terms of symptoms placed between the world and oneself, or in terms of passages à l’acte). Culture would refer to the work or discipline that each person offers to his body in order to make it supple, relax it, take care of it, and tend to it.

Counter-nature would then be any somatisation that the body might undergo.

Let us see what Denise Morel unfolds more specifically in her work Cancer and Psychoanalysis.

1 - D. Morel notes that a cancerous condition is rarely detected at its onset. Regularly, the painful and visible symptom points back to a tumour two or three years old: “it is therefore two or three years earlier in the patient’s history that one must look for the traumatic event”[7].

The trauma would proceed from an impossible representation, whether it be a representation of madness, of a separation, of death, of the loss of a loved one—a parent, a brother, or a sister—or “the irruption of an imaginary threatening a reactivation of an Oedipal fantasy”[8], thereby exposing the subject to castration.

Perhaps it is also because the traumatic event strikes the other, and not ourselves, that it forces all the more our imaginary and our capacities to represent this event to ourselves? And our capacities to delimit it. The loss or transformation of the image of the other’s body would be an event that forces open the gates of our imaginary. “The subject finds the cancerous somatic outlet when he cannot bear that his relation to the loved one (spouse, child, parent, or friend) should be in direct contact with death, with this ultimate and hitherto inadmissible castration”[9], which strikes that loved one in a real manner.

2 - Being confronted with this representation of a castration, this time a real one, would cause one to experience the threat of castration correlative to the representation, along with the anxiety that accompanies it.

The consequences of the trauma refer back to the real of death, and more particularly to a death anxiety so pervasive—or castration anxiety?—whether concerning the other or oneself, so pervasive that death ends up appearing intimately to the subject as “deliverance from tortures”[10]. As if the subject’s desire aspired only to relief, and to death, more than to anything else. The death drive would become dominant, in proportion to culpabilisation, which at times prevents any form of pleasure, if only by comparison with the one who is suffering, and likewise prevents a suicidal act, fantastically associated with relief.

3 - Thus, as D. Morel mentions, “how can one reproach the body for responding faithfully to this cry for help?”[11]. Somatisation would then appear as a compromise: rather than yielding completely to death (in a way forbidden because it would do violence to others), the subject would unconsciously concede to the death of a part of himself.

4 - The question emerging from these advances might be: “why, at a given moment in its history, does a particular organism no longer respond with appropriate defences?”[12] The terms “mechanisms of defence” lend themselves here to somatic and psychic equivocation.

D. Morel evokes the profound insecurity of subjects who have lost a close relative to cancer, mentioning the mechanisms of defence that come in response to the fantasies mobilised by this lived experience: undoing of a “perception dangerous to the ego”, magical thinking (“do not think about it, above all do not speak of it”[13] and it will not happen), disturbances in the perception of one’s body, one’s pains, and one’s emotions, and negation: so many processes of scotomisation of anxiety-provoking perceptions, sometimes reinforced by the more or less tacit agreement of one’s circle.

The appearance of the tumour would also be correlative to a narcissistic withdrawal. With the support of all the subject’s affective investment disappearing, a containing function also disappears for him. Does this mean that the subject’s body is narcissistically decathected, and likewise in the associated dimensions of pleasure (sensations, perceptions, proprioceptions)? Blind, boundless, Other jouissance, rather than phallic jouissance of one’s body in itself?

“Cancer is therefore the means placed at our disposal to authenticate this imaginary (to remain faithful to a fusional imaginary); it is a way (…) of lending credence to the omnipotence of the imaginary. Are we so far from psychotic delusion? Morbid somatisation then seems to be an enactment of fantasy (…)”[14]

The self/other difference does not exist or is disavowed, leaving no room for thought, for singular representation.

4 - Rather than hating and rejecting the bearer of suffering/symptom, the “causer” of suffering, as a mortiferous object, far too close and moreover already damaged, it is oneself who becomes the object of rejection: “a certain libidinal inversion occurs which maintains the loved one in the position of the ‘good object’, and tips the subject himself into the position of a ‘bad object’ to be destroyed. (…) The other scene of the murder unfolds in a physiological setting. Perceptions and affects then find themselves radically severed from the psyche, and the somatic explosion ensues.”[15]. As if the stake became dying so as not to hate, dying rather than hating. When the foreign, the strange, the unthinkable, death, take hold of the other, it is subsequently as though the anarchic, mad cancerous cell became the figure of that foreignness, that strangeness, that unthinkability, that death. “(… In) an inverted anaclitic reaction, the subject incorporates this external cancer; he takes into himself this ‘foreign body’ that assaults him and absorbs him entirely!”[16].

5 - To hate would bring culpabilisation onto the stage. Rather than assuming being guilty—and thus excluded from the family myth, from the fusional myth, from an imaginary that holds things together and confers consistency—the subject would unconsciously choose to be cut off: cut off from a part of himself in this instance, cut off from his body.

The sacrifice would be that of the body. Or of a part of it. Correlative to narcissistic withdrawal.

“(…) we may suppose that by unconsciously destroying his own body through cancer, it is the body of the other, and quite particularly the maternal body, that is targeted”[17], adds D. Morel. Body also refers metaphorically to the notion of the group—the family group with its members, for example. Or the couple, another version of the group, the most restricted, and possibly also the most fusional.

The subject suffering from cancer, if he testifies to his non-access to symbolic castration—perhaps a temporary non-access—would testify to an attempt at metaphorisation of a suffering fusional body.

Or, at any rate, an attempt to symbolise something of death.

This symbolisation appears as a compromise formation, grappling with the confused culpabilisation at play. Symbolisation right against the body, and even in and through the body, via a somatic symptom.

This progress, in spite of ourselves.

Anne-Gaëlle Burban, March 2013

The dialectic of nature / counter-nature gives rise to the question of the continuity and evolution of the human species within its environment. This ecology in progress never ceases to toss us back and forth in a becoming, making us deploy treasures of ingenuity to adapt to constraints and mutations that very often arise from the consequences of our socio-economic management of our presence in the world.

In view of technological, social, artistic, and intellectual advances, can one speak of the progress of humanity? And if so, how should we define this notion (and why not this motion)? Why have we become what we are?

What is certain is that what drives us forward, to go further in order to advance*, brings us at times jouissance, yet also lack, dissatisfaction, and frustration. This lingering taste of "come back for more", this narcissistic wound of humanity, this objet petit a, otherwise known as the Freudian Thing, propels us into a perpetual headlong flight forward and into a state of expectation that alienates us to the response of the other (this is the discourse of the hysteric: dH). In other words, it is the necessary and existential anxiety that has kept us alive for millennia.

It is a little as though we, denatured and Sisyphean animals, walked with our backs to the sun and tirelessly sought to recover our shadow. This image also echoes that of the unreachable star of which poets sometimes sing melancholically, as of a utopia that, ultimately, one must above all never lay to rest through mourning.

From this forward march are born languages, ambitions, curiosities, creative solutions, and innovations that superficially distance us from our state of nature. Superficially, because the human being seems to possess that astonishing capacity, as Freud showed in Totem and Taboo, to cultivate and conjugate in the present tense the primate and the millennia-old bacteria that lie dormant within us. In this sense, one might even argue that neurosis is a sign of progress, insofar as the subject seeks an escape, a symptom to wrap around their drives and adapt, as far as possible, to the laws of the city.

However, it sometimes happens that the machine seizes up and we fall into a state of melancholia or depression. Individually or collectively, we experience blockages or crises that give us occasions to halt our forward movement only to stutter on the spot.

And what if the way out lay in symbolisation, in the production of new signifiers?

When one examines Jacques Lacan's 4 discourses, one understands that discourse too can evolve and cause us to shift our positioning in our relation to the Other. Historically and broadly in the West (and elsewhere?), one might say that across the last five thousand years we have collectively passed from the discourse of the master (dM) to the discourse of the university (dU) with the Renaissance and the Age of Enlightenment, arriving at the Freudian discovery of the unconscious and the birth of the discourse of the analyst (dA). Individually, it is otherwise. Indeed, our relation to the world is barred. We are at once conscious beings and beings driven by the dynamics of our unconscious.

Therefore, if our unconscious is structured like a language and functions like an archival system, we are all bearers of another logic, in which our signifiers link together in spite of us to speak a discourse other than the one we believe we master in a state of consciousness. This state of nature, one might say, sometimes leads us to regress, yet it also bears our fundamental desire for being-in-the-world, for which the purpose of life is life.

The analytic cure therefore pursues this objective of providing a place, a heterotopia (first material, with the couch, and immaterial, with the protocol of the analyst's free-floating listening) to move the subject forward in the knowledge and (re)construction of their own discourse. Somewhat in the manner of the archaeologist, the analyst brings signifying chains and unconscious links back to the surface to help us free ourselves from them and give form to our good sense (that of our desire).

To go further in illustrating this idea, reading Freud's text on "Delusions and Dreams in Jensen's Gradiva" can prove to be a very fine journey to the heart of the "cure of love".

THE TALENT OF THE LITTLE POTS

Anne-Gaëlle Burban, May 2013

Virtual simulation for the visual art intervention project entitled Nature/Against Nature.

© Photo credit: Julien Borie, nOOrs.

Inside the vast space of an old barn, a crowd of 364 or 365 little glass pots (depending on the year), bearing or not bearing a coloured Post-it note in pink, yellow, orange, green, or blue, clusters directly on the floor and occupies the space by naturally forming a circular barrier 6 metres in diameter, thereby outlining an immense, vacant spherical area.

In the silence of the place, this in-situ installation plays with the plastic qualities of a unit (the little glass pot) that repeats itself and is each time neither wholly the same nor wholly another. Indeed, micro-variations punctuate the apprehension of the whole and operate locally as so many singular agents. Among these variants, one may notably cite the presence or absence of Post-it notes inside, their colour, their content, and their position. We will also be attentive to the shapes, as well as to the orientation and the way in which each pot captures and transmits light to our gaze.

Contrary to our mental image of an art gallery, the occupation—or rather the spatial deployment—takes place here horizontally rather than vertically. It is a relatively flat monument (around 8 to 10 cm depending on the height of the pots), acting somewhat like a bas-relief or a potentially sharp-edged puddle that prevents, or at least conditions in a certain way, the viewer's wandering.

Upon entering, the spectator might be struck by the sense of the uncanny emanating from this ephemeral installation. Indeed, the little glass yoghurt pot, a well-known companion of our table, freed from its foil lid, finds itself diverted from its function. From one, it passes to 365 and becomes the marker of passing time.

Caught up in the installation, each subject can identify with a little pot, full or empty, and feel their condition as a "little dot/pot" imprisoned by the herd instinct in the immensity of the cosmos.

The little pots seem determined by a law, a taboo, a fundamental fear preventing them from crossing an invisible boundary. Is this not how our societies and our individualities are governed? Is it the mark of a collective wisdom?

The contrast of the disciplined multitude of little pots creating this void can also provoke a feeling of unease, or even anxiety. From this anxiety a magical image—a fantasy—can be born. Indeed, nothing prevents us from attributing shamanic virtues to this sacred (because apparently virgin) zone.

In a certain way, the Nature/Against Nature installation seeks to awaken the ambivalence that resides within each of us. At once fascinated and repelled by this perimeter of the void and of lack, the subject passively observes the exaggerated multiplication of an everyday detail: the pot and the word. The repetition, the refrain of the module, can border on stuttering (OCD) or the symptom, or even on the cancerous proliferation of cells in a protean space of which we would be merely a tiny part. This nothingness, this fortress of the void, may also refer to the discourse of a certain capitalism that produces nothingness in place of desire and thus keeps the hystericised populace away from an invested jouissance.

At the same time, the idea of the multiplication of the pots (and not the loaves!) can also refer to the life/death dialectic, giving the advantage to Eros. It is then the parable of continuity, of resilience, of generations following one another since the dawn of time and confirming the thesis that the purpose of life is life.

As for the place of language in this work, it is central. The words contained within the pots are like talents revealed or yet to be revealed (in every sense of the term: currency and aptitudes). It is these words, with what is half-said or left unsaid in them, that bind and animate the multiple units into a whole. Like a horizontal Wailing Wall, each Post-it locally and individually contains a secret (a taboo) contributing globally to the cultural foundations (the Big Other) and to the collective enrichment of signifiers.

Thus, what would be fundamentally against nature would be the disappearance of these signifiers. Now, a society running short of new signifiers is a society gnawed away by the cancer of its own morbidity and doomed to imminent extinction.
